45:8.text: And Jesus answered and said unto him, Blessed art thou, Simon Barjona: for flesh and blood hath not revealed it unto thee, but my Father which is in heaven.

provenance.other: 'Blessed art thou' occurs in five KJV verses, which alone would not identify a source; but 'unto him, Blessed art thou' occurs in exactly one, Matthew 16:17, and Alma 45:8 reads 'Then Alma saith unto him, Blessed art thou'. The phrase appears fourteen times in the Book of Mormon and three times earlier in Alma (8:15, 19:10, 19:12); none of those follows a confession of Christ, and this one does.
provenance.significance: The evidence is the sequence, not the salutation. Matthew 16 runs: a question put to a disciple ('But whom say ye that I am?'), the disciple's confession ('Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God'), and then the blessing addressed to him by name. Alma 45:2-8 runs the same three steps twice over — 'Believest thou the words which I spake unto thee concerning those records?' / 'Yea, I believe'; 'Believest thou in Jesus Christ, which shall come?' / 'Yea, I believe all the words which thou hast spoken' — and closes with 'Then Alma saith unto him, Blessed art thou.' Recover Matthew's context and the blessing is followed immediately by the commission of a successor: 'thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church … I will give unto thee the keys.' Alma 45 does exactly that, and does it in the same order: blessing at 45:8, prophecy entrusted at 45:9 with an instruction to write and to withhold, and at 45:20-22 Helaman going out to establish the church in every city and appoint priests and teachers. The Book of Mormon has used this passage for a succession before — at 1 Nephi 2:1 and Mosiah 26:15 — but this is the place where it takes the whole shape of Matthew 16:15-19 and not merely the greeting.

45:8.note: 'Then Alma saith unto him, Blessed art thou; and the Lord shall prosper thee in this land.' Filed at 45:8 rather than at the phrase's first appearance in the book because what carries the row is the catechism in front of it: five verses of question-and-confession culminating in a named blessing, which is Matthew 16:15-17's structure and not a formula the Book of Mormon repeats elsewhere. The four-word run 'unto him, Blessed art thou' is a KJV singleton and belongs to that verse. The 1830 reads 'saith' where 1920 reads 'said', which keeps the historic present the KJV uses at this kind of turn.

45:11.text: For nation shall rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom: and there shall be famines, and pestilences, and earthquakes, in divers places.

provenance.other: 'Famines and pestilences' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 24:7 and Luke 21:11, and nowhere else; 'wars and rumours of wars' in exactly two, Matthew 24:6 and Mark 13:7. Alma 45:11 is the only verse in Alma that uses 'famines' at all. The Book of Mormon inverts the pair — 'wars and pestilences, yea, famines and bloodshed' — where both synoptic verses read famines first.
provenance.significance: The Olivet discourse is a prediction of the destruction of Jerusalem which the Book of Mormon has been mining since 1 Nephi 12:2 for predictions of the destruction of the Nephites, and Alma 45:10-14 is the fullest of them: four hundred years from Christ's appearance, dwindling in unbelief, wars and pestilences and famines, a generation that shall not all pass away before the iniquity comes, and a remnant that survives by being absorbed into the enemy. Every one of those is a move Matthew 24 makes — including 'this generation shall not pass, till all these things be fulfilled' (24:34), which Alma 45:12's 'the fourth generation shall not all pass away' answers by lengthening the interval and keeping the idiom. What the Book of Mormon does that the source cannot is give the prophecy a date and then narrate its fulfilment, which is the burden of the four books after this one.

45:11.note: 'Then shall they see wars and pestilences, yea, famines and bloodshed, even until the people of Nephi shall become extinct.' The pair 'famines and pestilences' is a two-verse KJV rarity and the surrounding sentence keeps the Olivet frame — a prophecy delivered privately, at a request to know when, running from wars through famine to a generation-count. Recorded across the book boundary under ADJUDICATING §4; the argument for Matthew 24 as the Book of Mormon's apocalyptic vocabulary is made at 1 Nephi 12:2 and 2 Nephi 10:6. What is new here is that the borrowing is put into the mouth of Alma as a private prophecy to a single son, with an instruction that it not be published until fulfilled (45:9) — which is not how Matthew 24 is delivered and is how apocalyptic literature says it was.

45:14.text: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the LORD:

provenance.other: 'Great and dreadful day' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Joel 2:31 and Joel 3:14's nearest equivalents read 'the great and the terrible day of the LORD' and 'the day of the LORD is near in the valley of decision'; the adjective 'dreadful' in this phrase is Malachi's alone. The Book of Mormon uses the phrase twice: here, and at 3 Nephi 25:5, which is inside the transcribed Malachi 3-4 block. Alma 45:14 is therefore the only free-standing use in the book, and it precedes the transcription by four books.
provenance.significance: Recover the context and Malachi 4:5 is not a threat but a provision: before the great and dreadful day the LORD undertakes to send Elijah, so that the earth is not smitten with a curse. Alma 45 takes the day and drops the provision — the great and dreadful day at 45:14 is the one on which the Nephites are wiped out, and the very next verse has Alma blessing the earth 'for the righteous' sake' and then, at 45:16, pronouncing exactly the curse Malachi 4:6 says Elijah's coming exists to prevent. And then, four verses on, a prophet leaves the land, is never heard of again, and is said to have been taken up. The chapter has the Malachi sequence in it — the dreadful day, the curse on the land, a prophet who does not die where anyone can find him — with the sending reversed into a departure.

45:14.note: 'Whosoever remaineth, and is not destroyed in that great and dreadful day.' A KJV singleton reproduced entire, used here for the destruction of a people rather than for the day of the LORD, and used four books before the Book of Mormon transcribes the chapter it comes from. Filed high on rarity. The reading offered in `significance` — that 45:14-19 runs the whole of Malachi 4 in altered order — is a proposal in the sense of CONVENTIONS §0a and rests on the sequence, not on further wording.

45:16.text: Thou art of purer eyes than to behold evil, and canst not look on iniquity: wherefore lookest thou upon them that deal treacherously, and holdest thy tongue when the wicked devoureth the man that is more righteous than he?

provenance.other: 'Canst not look on iniquity' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and so does 'purer eyes' — the same verse, Habakkuk 1:13. The Book of Mormon's rendering — 'the Lord cannot look upon sin with the least degree of allowance' — is a hapax in the Book of Mormon: 'least degree of allowance' occurs at Alma 45:16 and nowhere else in the book, though the sentence became one of the most quoted in it. The catalogue's earlier row at 1 Nephi 10:21 pairs Psalm 5:4 with Habakkuk 1:13 for 'no unclean thing can dwell with God'; this is the first place the Book of Mormon renders Habakkuk's clause itself.
provenance.significance: The metalepsis here is unusually sharp, because Habakkuk 1:13 is not a doctrinal statement at all — it is the opening of a complaint. The prophet says God cannot look on iniquity precisely in order to ask why he is doing so: 'wherefore lookest thou upon them that deal treacherously, and holdest thy tongue when the wicked devoureth the man that is more righteous than he?' The clause is a premise in an accusation about divine inaction while an invading army destroys the righteous. Alma 45:16 lifts it out of the complaint and makes it the ground of a curse — the reason the land will be destroyed when its people are fully ripe — in a chapter that has just come through a war and is predicting the extinction of the righteous nation. Habakkuk's question, in other words, is the question Alma 45:10-14 has just answered in advance: the wicked will devour the more righteous, and it will be allowed. The Book of Mormon uses the premise and declines the protest.

45:16.note: 'For the Lord cannot look upon sin with the least degree of allowance.' No clause is reproduced, but the proposition and its shape are Habakkuk 1:13's, and Habakkuk 1:13 is the only KJV verse that states it — the two strings that carry it, 'purer eyes' and 'canst not look on iniquity', are both singletons there. What the Book of Mormon adds is the quantifier: 'with the least degree of allowance' is not biblical English and not Book of Mormon English elsewhere either, and it turns Habakkuk's absolute into a scale, which is what a doctrine of degrees of accountability needs. Filed as paraphrase rather than allusion for that reason.

45:19.text: And he buried him in a valley in the land of Moab, over against Bethpeor: but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day.

provenance.route: Deuteronomy 34:5-6, with the assumption tradition that stands behind Jude 1:9 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: Moses is named outright, so the source is not in doubt; the question the verse raises is which claim about Moses it is making. Deuteronomy 34:5-6 says Moses died and that the LORD buried him — 'he buried him in a valley in the land of Moab … but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day' — which is the second of the two options Alma 45:19 offers ('buried by the hand of the Lord'). No KJV verse says the first. The clause 'God took him' occurs in exactly one KJV verse and its subject is Enoch (Genesis 5:24, glossed at Hebrews 11:5 as translation 'that he should not see death'); Elijah's going up by a whirlwind is 2 Kings 2:11. Jude 1:9 is the only verse in the Bible that touches an afterlife for the body of Moses at all, and it does so at second hand, reporting a dispute between Michael and the devil over it — the fragment of the extra-canonical Assumption of Moses that survived into the New Testament canon.
provenance.alternative: Read strictly, 45:19 may intend only Deuteronomy 34:6 — 'the Lord took Moses unto himself' as a loose paraphrase of God burying him where nobody can find the grave — in which case the verse is not appealing to an assumption tradition at all and the Jude connection is ours, not the text's.
provenance.significance: Alma 45:19 makes an explicit appeal to a text: 'But behold, the Scripture saith the Lord took Moses unto himself.' No scripture says it. Deuteronomy 34:5 says the opposite in as many words — 'So Moses the servant of the LORD died there in the land of Moab' — and 34:6 supplies a burial and a lost grave, which is why the verse has to offer the reader both options before choosing. The only biblical hint that Moses did not simply stay buried is Jude 1:9, and Jude gets it from a book that is not in the canon. So this verse is doing something the rest of the catalogue rarely catches: it is citing, as scripture, a tradition the King James Bible transmits only as the residue of a lost apocryphon, and it is using it to license a matching claim about its own prophet. The apparatus of the sentence is the tell — 'the saying went abroad in the church', 'the Scripture saith', 'we suppose', 'we know nothing' — a narrator reasoning from a disputed proof-text to a conclusion he marks as inference. And the two figures the KJV actually does take up, Enoch and Elijah, are the two the verse does not name, though Genesis 5:24's 'God took him' is the sentence its 'the Lord took Moses unto himself' is built out of.

45:19.note: 'He was taken up by the spirit, or buried by the hand of the Lord, even as Moses. But behold, the Scripture saith the Lord took Moses unto himself.' The second half of Alma's disappearance is Deuteronomy 34:5-6 — a prophet who leaves, dies out of sight, is buried by God, and whose sepulchre no man knows — and the chapter reproduces that verse's effect exactly at 45:18, 'as to his death or his burial, we know not of'. The first half is not in the Bible. The narrator's own citation formula is what makes the row valuable: he says the Scripture says a thing the Scripture does not say, and the nearest the canon comes to saying it is Jude 1:9's report of a quarrel over Moses's body, itself a quotation from outside the canon. Confidence is certain as to dependence on Deuteronomy 34 (Moses is named and the burial is the point); the Jude element is recorded as the tradition the verse's claim requires, not as a verbal borrowing. `mediation` is left uncertain because tools/mediation-check.py finds no point at which the OT and NT candidates differ and the Book of Mormon follows one of them — the two texts are not parallel versions of one saying, so the verse cannot settle its own route.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Alma 45.19 (cross-references Deuteronomy 34:5-6 and Jude 1:9)
